Chapter 3: Sensory Worlds and Emotional Lives
Have you ever wondered how someone else experiences the world?
Every living creature, whether it’s a person or an animal, sees, hears, and feels things through their senses—yet, not all senses work the same way. For animals, and for folks with autism, the sensory world can be more intense, more immediate, and sometimes just overwhelming. That shapes not only what they notice around them, but also how they feel—and how they act.
Imagine a parent at a busy birthday party, watching their child. The noise and excitement start piling up until it’s just too much—the kid covers their ears and slips away to a quiet corner. Other kids barely notice the chaos. But for this child, the sounds are just too much to handle.
The parent remembers a similar moment at the vet’s office—not with their child, but with their dog. The sound of electric clippers made the dog tremble, even though the haircut itself didn’t hurt at all. In both cases, it’s not stubbornness or fear—it’s sensory overload.
Let’s take a closer look at what’s going on here. The science of sensory processing tells us that animals and autistic people often have heightened sensitivity to certain sights, sounds, or smells. A sudden noise, a bright light, or a strong scent can trigger a huge reaction—it’s not a decision, just how their nervous systems are wired. They’re tuned in differently, picking up more from their environment than most of us ever realize.
Now, this kind of sensitivity can be stressful, but it’s not all bad. In fact, it can be a big advantage. Animals depend on their senses for survival. Catching a faint sound or a subtle scent can mean the difference between safety and danger. Picture a horse tensing up when it hears something far away, ready to bolt if it needs to. Or a dog picking up the scent of a stranger, instantly alert to something we’d never notice. These instincts? They’re automatic—built by evolution to keep them safe.
For someone with autism, though, these sensitivities can make daily life feel like a minefield. Busy places, loud noises, an unexpected brush on the arm—any of these can be overwhelming. But there’s a flip side: they often notice things others miss. Maybe it’s the texture of a sweater, the rhythm of someone’s footsteps, or sunlight dancing across a wall. Sometimes those details soothe. Other times, they just add to the stress. It all depends on the moment.
Let’s go back to the woman working in the cattle yard. She learns to pay close attention to what the animals are sensing. She discovers that even small changes—a fresh coat of paint, a different kind of flooring—can make a world of difference. By designing spaces that respect these sensitivities, she’s able to lower stress and help the animals feel safer, happier, and more at ease.
But what about the emotional side? A lot of people still think animals don’t really have feelings, or that their emotions are simple—just basic instinct. But the evidence tells a different story. Animals feel fear, joy, frustration—even empathy. Their emotions are deeply tied to what they sense, and to the bonds they form with each other.
Picture a dog pacing and whining when its owner leaves the house. It’s not just reacting to the empty room—it’s feeling a kind of loss, shaped by its connection with that person. Stories like this play out every day, whether in a barn, a living room, or out in the wild. Animals form relationships and experience a whole range of emotions, just like we do.
So what’s the key takeaway here? If we make the effort to understand the sensory and emotional worlds of animals—and people with autism—we can create spaces that are more humane and supportive. It’s not just about being kind. It’s about recognizing just how rich and complex other minds really are.
And that awareness? It’s the first step toward real empathy.
